title: Feed line impedance, loss and SWR
blurb: Work out SWR from load and line impedance, and explain how line loss and tuners change what you measure.

G9A01.why: Z₀ comes from conductor **spacing and radius**. Length and frequency don't change it.

G9A02.why: Reflected power makes extra trips along the line, so a **high SWR increases loss** in a lossy line.
G9A02.trap: Loss and SWR are linked, not independent.

G9A03.why: Window line (ladder line with windows cut in its web) is nominally **450 Ω**. Common coax is 50 or 75 Ω.

G9A04.why: Power reflects where **line impedance and feed point impedance differ**. A match reflects nothing.
G9A04.trap: Resonance and unbalanced lines don't by themselves cause reflection.

G9A05.why: Coax **attenuation increases** as frequency goes up.

G9A06.why: Feed line loss is rated in **decibels per 100 feet**, then scaled to your real length.

G9A07.why: No standing waves only if the antenna impedance **equals the line's Z₀**. Line length can't fix that.
G9A07.trap: Quarter-wave line lengths transform impedance, they don't stop reflection.

G9A08.why: The tuner only fixes what the radio sees. The antenna mismatch is unchanged, so the line still carries **5:1**.

G9A09.trap: SWR is never written below 1, so 1:4 can't be right.

G9A10.trap: A low load gives the same kind of SWR as a high one: always larger over smaller.

G9A11.why: Line loss absorbs the reflected wave on its way back, so the SWR at the line input reads **lower** than at the antenna.
